A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OCC-to-unsupervised anomaly filtering work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, support comparison despite isolated naming and reporting inconsistencies.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark experiments, hyperparameter and corruption-rate analyses, qualitative comparisons, and supplementary experiments on ensemble filtering.

after.justification: v2 retains original image and video experiments and adds a broader OCC comparison and a category-concentrated anomaly corruption experiment.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains disjoint random subsets, independently trained OCC models, predictions on other subsets, weighted two-Gaussian thresholds, majority voting, and final retraining. Folding is renamed BAAF and explained through bagging. The unchanged video adaptation moves from Section 3.4 to supplementary Section 8.1.

E1.justification: MVTec AD, VisA, LOCO AD, and Peds2 remain covered, including video results relocated to the appendix. v2 adds a category-concentrated anomaly distribution intended to test dependence between anomalous samples, extending the previous randomly sampled corruption scenarios.

E2.justification: Table 2 expands from three to eight OCC comparisons, adding PatchCore within this comparison and introducing Dfm, Fastflow, and PaDiM evaluations. v2 separately reports AnomalyDino and Dinomaly; the exact correspondence of v1's 'DinoAnomaly' entry is ambiguous because its citation identifies Dinomaly. The other principal comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The new dependence experiment selects the largest anomaly category per class plus 'combined' anomalies, averages 12% contamination, and uses BAAF(1/4), whereas the retained random-corruption sweep uses (3/6). The speed discussion changes the stated main configuration from three votes/four folds to one vote/four bags, although Table 1 remains (3/4); this does not establish that existing experiments were rerun. Shared preprocessing, metrics, and overlapping evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Section 4.6 and Table 5 add an explicit test of category-concentrated anomalies, reporting detection performance and filtering precision/recall to examine the independence assumption. The existing hyperparameter grid, corruption-rate sweep, ensemble experiment, filtering of already-unsupervised methods, and qualitative cases are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The votes in both algorithms are filtering hyperparameters rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 Table 2 adds substantial model-level results and an eight-model average I-AUROC of 0.933 with BAAF versus 0.762 without it at 10% corruption. The new Table 5 scenario reports I-AUROC 0.978, P-AUROC 0.972, and AUPRO 0.931. v1's DinoAnomaly wrapped entry reports 0.978, whereas v2's AnomalyDino entry reports 0.951; conflicting citations prevent treating this confidently as a same-method decline. Most earlier benchmark and appendix values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.1 adds explicit distributional modeling assumptions: approximately uniform anomalies outside the nominal region and multivariate-Gaussian nominal data. Independent and identically distributed sampling is also made explicit. The three central equations and near-zero similar-anomaly-pair corollary remain substantively unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The universal OCC transformation, state-of-the-art image benchmark claims, and first fully unsupervised logical anomaly detection claim remain. v2 focuses the title and abstract on images and adds an explicit contribution claiming an average 0.171 I-AUROC improvement across eight OCC methods. Video evidence remains in the appendix.

C2.justification: v2 adds a bagging-based regularization explanation and interprets the new concentrated-corruption experiment as evidence of sensitivity to independence violations. Its claimed worsening relative to random 20% corruption conflicts with the displayed I-AUROC values, 0.978 versus 0.972, and the configurations differ. The stated training-time limitation also narrows from 4–40 times to 5–13 times, while the broader configuration grid remains.

D1.justification: Supplementary Sections 12.9–12.13 newly specify official PUAD code and Anomalib default recipes for Dinomaly, Dfm, Fastflow, and PaDiM, including removal of test-based early stopping. Earlier implementation details, including FUN-AD's approximately 40,000 steps and the Reverse Distillation++ and DMAD training rules, are retained.

R1.justification: v1 presents the approach as dataset folding; v2 explicitly positions the central contribution as a modification and extension of Breiman's bagging, explaining sampling without replacement and using the ensemble for training-data filtering. Seven references are added, supporting this positioning, the statistical framework, and additional models. The relationship to established ensemble learning is substantially revised.

P1.justification: v2 extensively revises the abstract, introduction, framework discussion, and method exposition around BAAF and bagging terminology. Video methodology and results move into a dedicated supplementary section, experimental subsections are reordered, and future work and limitations become a separate section before the conclusion.

P2.justification: The document changes throughout from two-column to single-column layout, with figures and Algorithm 1 resized and relocated. Tables 2 and 3 are substantially restructured, Table 2 gains model rows and difference/average summaries, and the corruption table gains a dependence-test column. Existing qualitative images and Gaussian-fit plots are retained.

improvement.justification: The expanded OCC comparison and accompanying implementation notes strengthen support for the central generality claim, while the explicit connection to bagging clarifies research positioning. The new dependence experiment adds useful evidence, but its differing configurations and interpretation inconsistent with the reported AUROC limit its conclusions. These issues temper the empirical and explanatory gains, supporting a limited overall improvement.
